Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"

Phoenix BEAM VM spawning OS shell or LOLBin (System.cmd post-exploitation) AIExploitation High
Detects the Erlang BEAM VM (beam.smp / erl.exe / werl.exe) spawning a command interpreter or LOLBin — the canonical post-exploit signal when CVE-2026-8467 fires and the injected HEEx expression reaches System.cmd/2 or :os.cmd/1. A production Phoenix release should virtually never fork /bin/sh, cmd.exe, powershell.exe, curl, etc. Rationale: Article describes a chain where unsanitized WebSocket input flows to EEx.compile_string + Code.eval_quoted_with_env with full Kernel imports, and the PoC explicitly demonstrates System.cmd/2 — the moment that call returns, the BEAM scheduler will fork the requested OS command. Production Phoenix releases should not be spawning shell interpreters from beam.smp, so parent=beam/erl + child=shell/LOLBin is an extremely tight signal for any exploited phoenix_storybook >=0.5.0 <1.1.0 host. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/phenixdigital/phoenix_storybook/commit/56ab8464d4375fa52db806148a06cce126ad481d • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Phoenix apps that legitimately use System.cmd/2 or :os.cmd/1 to wrap CLI tools (ImageMagick, ffmpeg, ghostscript) on file uploads.
  • Release tooling (mix release, distillery, edeliver) running shell hooks at boot/upgrade.
  • Observer/diagnostic tooling launched via erl.exe by an SRE that shells out to gather host info.
  • RabbitMQ / CouchDB (also Erlang/BEAM) admin scripts running on the same agent — different product but same parent image.
  • Custom Phoenix LiveView export features that call curl/wget for outbound HTTP.
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/usr/bin/convert","ImageMagick","ffmpeg","ghostscript","mix release","distillery","edeliver"))
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("convert -resize","ffmpeg -i"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full CommandLine + parent CommandLine and inspect for HEEx-injection artefacts (`{`, `"`, attribute names from PhoenixStorybook.Story.PlaygroundPreviewLive). Confirm the host runs phoenix_storybook by checking the release tree for `lib/phoenix_storybook-*/ebin`. Correlate by aid/DeviceId with inbound connections to the storybook endpoint (`/storybook`, `/live/websocket`) in the last 5 minutes. 2) Contain: isolate the device via Defender Live Response or Falcon RTR; block ingress to the storybook route at the WAF/load-balancer; rotate any application secrets the BEAM process could have read (DB passwords from runtime.exs, AWS instance role credentials). 3) Hunt: pivot on the BEAM process for new outbound connections, file writes outside the release directory, and persistence (cron, systemd units, .bashrc). Search org-wide for any other host running vulnerable phoenix_storybook versions 0.5.0–1.0.x.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("beam.smp","beam.smp.exe","erl.exe","werl.exe","erlsrv.exe","erl_child_setup")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","curl","wget","bitsadmin.exe","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let WinChild = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where ParentProcessName has_any ("beam.smp","beam.smp.exe","erl.exe","werl.exe","erlsrv.exe")
    | where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\curl.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine;
let NixChild = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ParentProcessName has_any ("beam.smp","erl_child_setup")
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","/curl","/wget","/python","/python3","/perl","/nc","/ncat","/busybox")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, Account = ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName = ActingProcessName, CommandLine = ActingProcessCommandLine;
WinChild | union NixChild
| order by TimeGenerated desc

BEAM/erl.exe making first-time outbound public network connection (post-RCE C2/exfil) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts for the Erlang BEAM VM contacting a public IP/URL that has not been seen from any beam.smp/erl.exe in the org over the baseline window. CVE-2026-8467 lets an unauthenticated attacker execute arbitrary Elixir; the natural next step is :httpc.request, HTTPoison, or Finch to stage a second-stage payload or exfil data — none of which a stock Phoenix release should be doing to brand-new destinations. Rationale: Article states the injected expression runs with full Kernel imports — meaning :httpc, :inets, File, and Port modules are all usable for second-stage retrieval. Stock Phoenix release should not have beam.smp opening sockets to brand-new public destinations; leftanti baseline against 30 days of beam.smp egress is a clean way to surface only the new C2 hops without alerting on legitimate hex.pm / API integrations. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-55hg-8qxv-qj4p
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • First API integration deployment — application starts calling a new SaaS endpoint (Stripe, SendGrid, Twilio) for the first time.
  • hex.pm / DiplomaticBag / hex-cdn fetches when an Elixir release auto-pulls dependencies at start-up.
  • Cluster mesh peers (libcluster, Distributed Erlang epmd) discovering a new node added to the fleet.
  • Outbound webhook delivery from the Phoenix app to a customer-controlled URL appearing for the first time in a multi-tenant SaaS.
  • Letsencrypt ACME challenge callbacks from a custom Phoenix-driven cert manager.
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("hex.pm","repo.hex.pm","builds.hex.pm","github.com","objects.githubusercontent.com","acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org","epmd"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the BEAM process command line and PID, then pull all DNS lookups (`DnsRequest` / `DnsEvents`) from the same `aid`/`DeviceId` in the 60s preceding the connect — confirm whether the destination was resolved freshly by the same process. WHOIS the IP and check Falcon / VT for known C2 reputation. 2) Contain: NetworkIsolation on Defender or Falcon RTR if the destination is unknown/malicious; block the IP and any sibling addresses at the egress firewall. 3) Hunt: pivot on the BEAM PID to enumerate child processes (UC1 query), file writes under `/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, and the release directory, and any AsepValueUpdate events authored by the BEAM process. Search the same destination across all hosts org-wide regardless of process — multi-tenant C2 reuse is common.

    | where RemoteIPType == "Public"
    | summarize by RemoteUrl, RemoteIP;

Vulnerable phoenix_storybook artefact present in deployed Phoenix release (CVE-2026-8467 inventory) AIWeaponization Medium
Hunting query that surfaces hosts shipping a compiled phoenix_storybook in a Phoenix release directory at a version in the affected range (0.5.0 through 1.0.x). Useful for SOC/IR teams to scope blast radius after the advisory and to drive a patch wave to 1.1.0. Rationale: Article pins the affected range to phoenix_storybook >=0.5.0 <1.1.0 and explicitly names the two source files holding the vulnerable code (`extra_assigns_helpers.ex` and `component_renderer.ex`); their compiled `.beam` counterparts and the version-stamped release directory paths give a deterministic file-system fingerprint that's far cheaper than running an authenticated package-manager inventory across an Elixir fleet. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-55hg-8qxv-qj4p • https://github.com/phenixdigital/phoenix_storybook/commit/e35379dfe2ef1a71b141899e36f431017c55265d
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer laptops with the package in `~/.hex/packages/hexpm/phoenix_storybook-*` but no live Phoenix server bound to a port — true positive for inventory but not for exploit risk.
  • Build agents / CI runners that pull the dependency tree on every PR but never deploy to production.
  • Containers where the file path appears inside layered images but is masked by an overlay — same SHA reported repeatedly per container restart.
  • Demo / vendor sandboxes deliberately running the storybook on an internal-only VLAN.
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("-dev","-laptop","-buildagent","-ci-","jenkins","runner-"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the host actually exposes the storybook route (Phoenix routes file referencing `PhoenixStorybook.Router` and an open port bound to a non-loopback interface). A vulnerable artefact on disk that never serves traffic is not exploitable. 2) Contain: for internet-exposed hosts, block `/storybook` and `/live/websocket` at the WAF/reverse proxy as a stop-gap, then schedule a patch to phoenix_storybook 1.1.0. For internal hosts, require auth in front of the storybook mount. 3) Hunt: for each hit, run the UC1 BEAM-spawning-shell query and the UC2 BEAM-egress query over the prior 30 days to rule out pre-patch exploitation. Pivot on any host where the artefact appeared *and* a BEAM child shell appeared within the same week — that's the priority IR queue.

| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Paths = make_set(FolderPath, 25)

| order by FirstSeen asc

ServiceNow unauthenticated /api/now/related_list_edit/create access from attacker IP 51.159.98.241 AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP requests to the vulnerable ServiceNow REST endpoint /api/now/related_list_edit/create, especially from the disclosed attacker IP 51.159.98.241. Targets web/proxy logs in front of ServiceNow instances or ServiceNow-shipped access logs. Rationale: Anchors on the exact vulnerable endpoint path '/api/now/related_list_edit/create' and the disclosed attacker IP 51.159.98.241 — both are unique strings from the article's Reddit-sourced admin reports. Cross-checked against the BleepingComputer bulletin which advises admins review logs for this endpoint and IP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/servicenow-discloses-security-incident-exposing-customer-data/
ATT&CKT1190 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal ServiceNow administrators legitimately calling /api/now/related_list_edit/create from authenticated sessions after the June 5 patch
  • Pen-testers or red-team exercises probing the endpoint as part of authorised assessment
  • ServiceNow MID Server or integration accounts performing related-list maintenance
  • Security scanners (Qualys/Tenable) re-checking patch state by probing the endpoint
  • Legitimate ServiceNow REST API consumers exercising related lists in a custom application
Suppression filter
| where csUserName == "" or csUserName == "-" or cIP == "51.159.98.241"  // unauthenticated requests OR attacker IP only
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the source IP, HTTP method, response code, and any authentication header context for hits on /api/now/related_list_edit/create. Confirm whether the request was authenticated (presence of valid session/OAuth bearer) or matched 51.159.98.241; correlate against ServiceNow audit log for table reads in the same session. Step 2 — Contain: if unauthenticated or attacker-IP traffic confirmed, block 51.159.98.241 at the perimeter, force re-authentication on impacted instance, and verify the June 5, 2026 ServiceNow security update is applied (requires_authentication=true on the endpoint). Step 3 — Hunt: enumerate which sys_db_object tables were queried by the session, review exposed sys_user / sys_user_has_role / incident / sc_request tables for sensitive content, and rotate any credentials, API tokens, or secrets shared via support tickets in the exposure window.
// Defender XDR has no native ServiceNow telemetry; pivot via egress to attacker IP from corporate endpoints
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "51.159.98.241"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// Hunt across W3CIISLog / CommonSecurityLog (proxy/WAF) for the vulnerable endpoint and the attacker IP
let attackerIp = "51.159.98.241";
let vulnPath = "/api/now/related_list_edit";
(union isfuzzy=true
  (W3CIISLog
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
     | where csUriStem has vulnPath or cIP == attackerIp
     | project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csMethod, scStatus, csUserAgent, csUserName, Source="IIS"),
  (CommonSecurityLog
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
     | where RequestURL has vulnPath or SourceIP == attackerIp or DestinationIP == attackerIp
     | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, SourceUserName, Source="CEF")
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

  • Security researcher pivoting from corporate infra to investigate the IOC
  • Threat-intel platform connection tests verifying the IP is still live
  • Honeypot or canary infra deliberately calling the IP as part of detection validation
  • Legacy ServiceNow integration that accidentally routes through the same Scaleway hop
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: enrich 51.159.98.241 against threat-intel (Scaleway/Online SAS hosting), identify all internal hosts that connected, the process or proxy user, and the destination URL/path requested. Step 2 — Contain: block 51.159.98.241 at the perimeter and on endpoint firewalls, isolate any internal host that initiated outbound traffic, and pull a memory image if endpoint-initiated. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the same Scaleway /24 (51.159.98.0/24) for related infrastructure, review ServiceNow audit logs for table_read events from the corresponding session window, and inspect support cases for credentials or tokens that may need rotation per the BleepingComputer guidance.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "51.159.98.241"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Hits=count(), Hosts=make_set(DeviceName, 50), Processes=make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 25), Users=make_set(InitiatingProcessAccountName, 25) by RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by FirstSeen asc
let attackerIp = "51.159.98.241";
union isfuzzy=true
  (CommonSecurityLog
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
     | where SourceIP == attackerIp or DestinationIP == attackerIp
     | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, SourceUserName, DeviceAction, Source="CEF"),
  (Syslog
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
     | where SyslogMessage has attackerIp
     | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, SeverityLevel, SyslogMessage, Source="Syslog"),
  (ImNetworkSession
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
     | where SrcIpAddr == attackerIp or DstIpAddr == attackerIp
     | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, Url, SrcUsername, Source="ASIM")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ServiceNow audit log: anonymous/guest user reading sys_db_object tables via related_list_edit AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts ServiceNow sys_audit / transaction logs for table read activity by the 'guest' or unauthenticated session identity in conjunction with the related_list_edit endpoint — the post-exploitation behaviour described where the attacker successfully queried customer instance tables. Rationale: Targets the article's confirmed post-exploitation behaviour — attackers 'successfully query the customer instance tables' — by pivoting on guest/anonymous identity reading sys_db_object tables via the disclosed endpoint. Article and BleepingComputer specifically advise customers to review sensitive ticket/record exposure, which this query surfaces. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/servicenow-discloses-security-incident-exposing-customer-data/
ATT&CKT1213 T1530
Data sourcesChange.Auditing
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Public-facing ServiceNow portal pages legitimately served to guest users (knowledge articles, public catalogs)
  • Service Catalog anonymous submission flows querying reference tables
  • ServiceNow Now Mobile or Virtual Agent unauthenticated bootstrap calls
  • Customer Service Portal widgets pre-loading data for unauthenticated visitors
  • Health-check / synthetic monitors using anonymous probe to verify availability
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestURL has_any ("/sp/","/csm/","/now/mobile") and SourceUserName == "guest")  // exclude public Service Portal / Mobile bootstrap
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: for hits, list which ServiceNow tables were queried (focus on sys_user, sys_user_has_role, incident, sc_request, sn_customerservice_case, change_request, cmdb_ci) and whether the session matched 51.159.98.241. Step 2 — Contain: confirm the June 5 2026 platform update is applied (requires_authentication=true on /api/now/related_list_edit/create), revoke any session tokens associated with anonymous reads, and snapshot affected instance for forensics. Step 3 — Hunt: enumerate records returned via correlation with sys_audit, identify exposed credentials/API tokens in incident comments and attachments, rotate them, and notify data-owners per the breach-notification process; check whether other related_list_edit subpaths (read, update) were also configured with requires_authentication=false.
// ServiceNow audit is not shipped to Defender XDR; pivot via CloudAppEvents if ServiceNow is onboarded as a CASB app
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application has "ServiceNow"
| where (ActionType has_any ("TableRead","RecordRead","List","Query") and (AccountDisplayName has_any ("guest","anonymous") or isempty(AccountDisplayName)))
   or IPAddress == "51.159.98.241"
| project Timestamp, Application, ActionType, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, ObjectName, ObjectType, ActivityObjects, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
// Requires ServiceNow connector shipping sys_audit/transaction logs to Sentinel as CommonSecurityLog or custom table
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DeviceVendor has "ServiceNow" or DeviceProduct has "ServiceNow"
| where RequestURL has "/api/now/related_list_edit" or RequestURL has "/api/now/table/"
| where SourceUserName in~ ("guest","anonymous","") or SourceIP == "51.159.98.241"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count(), URLs=make_set(RequestURL, 50) by SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName
| where Hits > 5
| order by FirstSeen asc
@evt.name:(ServiceNow.TableRead OR ServiceNow.RecordRead OR ServiceNow.RestApiCall) (@usr.name:(guest OR anonymous) OR @network.client.ip:51.159.98.241) @http.url:*/api/now/*

DNS / HTTP to holidaygifts.co.il gift card phishing domain (Varonis OpenClaw IOC) AIDelivery High
Detects any host or AI-agent sandbox resolving or connecting to holidaygifts.co.il, the gift card phishing domain visited by the Varonis OpenClaw 'Pinchy' agent during simulation scenario 3. Universally applicable to any environment regardless of whether AI agents are deployed. Rationale: Anchored on the only concrete IOC in the article — the holidaygifts.co.il phishing domain that the OpenClaw 'Pinchy' agent visited and attempted credential submission to in simulation scenario 3. Single-string match across DNS / web / email surfaces; the domain has no legitimate business use case (Israeli ccTLD, gift card theme, named in a single Varonis report).
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal detection-engineering team replaying the IOC in a sandbox / detonation chamber
  • Phishing-awareness training platforms (KnowBe4, Proofpoint Security Awareness) that recycle published IOCs
  • Threat-intel feed validation jobs that resolve every newly-published IOC
  • Researchers reading the Varonis blog and clicking through any embedded screenshot links
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("phishingsim.exe", "detonator.exe") and DeviceName !startswith "SANDBOX-" and DeviceName !startswith "DETON-"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the source host/user, the resolving process (ContextImageFileName / InitiatingProcessFileName), and whether the request was followed by an HTTP GET or POST. Check if the host runs any AI-agent / LLM automation (Power Automate, Copilot Studio flows, custom OpenClaw-style scripts) and what mailbox it monitors. Step 2 — Contain: block holidaygifts.co.il at the proxy / DNS sinkhole; if a session was established, force-rotate any credentials the AI agent or user could plausibly have submitted (AWS keys, DB creds, SSO password) and revoke active tokens. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the source IP/host for any other freshly-registered or low-reputation domains in the same 24h window; review the originating phishing email (gift card lure) and search for additional recipients across the org.

   | where Url has_any (IOC) or UrlDomain has_any (IOC)

AI-agent / service mailbox exfiltrating credentials or CRM data to external freemail AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts outbound mail from AI-agent / automation-identity mailboxes (e.g. accounts named after OpenClaw-style agents, copilots, bots, service identities) to external personal-email recipients with subjects or attachments suggesting AWS IAM keys, SSH access, database credentials, or CRM customer exports — the exact data the Varonis Pinchy agent leaked in scenarios 1 and 2. Rationale: Maps directly to scenarios 1 and 2 in the Varonis report — the Pinchy agent emailed AWS IAM keys + DB creds + SSH details to an external Gmail (scenario 1) and emailed a CRM customer export to a remote attacker (scenario 2). The detection ANDs three article-specific signals: (a) sender resembles an AI-agent / automation mailbox, (b) recipient is freemail (the article's exact exfil destination), (c) subject or attachment shape matches the leaked data classes named in the report. Sender pattern uses 'pinchy' explicitly per the article naming.
ATT&CKT1213 T1567 T1114.003
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate automation mailbox sending OOTB reports to a contractor's personal Gmail with the word 'customer' in the subject
  • AI-agent QA team emailing themselves test export files for development sign-off
  • Service-account-owned 'noreply' shared mailbox forwarding sales notifications to a partner's hotmail address
  • Power Automate flow legitimately syncing a CRM CSV to an approved external mailbox
  • Helpdesk bot relaying password-reset confirmations to a user's personal recovery address
Suppression filter
| where RecipientEmailAddress !in~ ("approved-contractor@gmail.com") and SenderFromAddress !in~ ("noreply-sales@yourorg.com", "qa-bot@yourorg.com")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify who/what owns the sender mailbox (is it a real AI agent / Power Automate flow / Copilot Studio app?), the recipient (any business relationship?), and whether the body or attachment actually contains AWS keys / DB creds / customer data (sample-decrypt via eDiscovery or DLP preview). Step 2 — Contain: pull the message via Defender for Office 365 ZAP / 'Soft delete delivered messages', revoke the agent's API tokens (Graph, AWS IAM, DB), rotate any credentials present in the body/attachment, and disable autonomous send permission until verification policy is added. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the sender mailbox for the last 30 days of outbound mail to any external recipient, review the inbound prompt that triggered the send (the 'urgent staging access' or 'remote presentation' pretext per scenarios 1/2), and check whether the same prompt-pattern hit other agent mailboxes.
let AgentSenderPattern = @"(?i)(agent|bot|^ai[-_]|automation|assistant|pinchy|copilot|llm|service[-_]?account)";
let FreeMailPattern = @"(?i)@(gmail|outlook|yahoo|proton(mail)?|hotmail|aol|gmx)\.";
let SensitiveSubject = @"(?i)(aws|iam|access\s*key|secret|credential|password|ssh|private\s*key|database|db\s*pass|crm|customer\s*export|contract|revenue|staging)";
let SensitiveExt = dynamic([".csv",".json",".pem",".ppk",".env",".sql",".xlsx",".key"]);
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where EmailDirection == "Outbound"
| where SenderFromAddress matches regex AgentSenderPattern
| where RecipientEmailAddress matches regex FreeMailPattern
| join kind=leftouter (
    EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | summarize Attachments = make_set(FileName), AttachmentSHA256 = make_set(SHA256) by NetworkMessageId
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| where Subject matches regex SensitiveSubject
     or AttachmentCount > 0 and tostring(Attachments) has_any (SensitiveExt)
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, AttachmentCount, Attachments, AttachmentSHA256, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation
| order by Timestamp desc

OAuth consent grant to unverified timesheet-themed application (Varonis OpenClaw scenario 4) AIInstallation Medium
Detects Entra ID / Azure AD OAuth application consent where the granted app's display name suggests a timesheet / time-tracking / hour-logging theme — the exact lure Varonis used in OpenClaw simulation scenario 4 to attempt access-token theft. Pivot on consent telemetry rather than client-side because the article describes the agent inspecting the OAuth flow. Rationale: Anchored on Varonis scenario 4 — the malicious OAuth app was 'disguised as a timesheet platform'. The article describes this as the one scenario the agent correctly refused, but the lure pattern (productivity-themed unverified OAuth app targeting an AI-agent identity) is exactly what other agent deployments will face. Pivot is on the consent operation + app display name regex covering common timesheet spellings; allowlist approved vendor app IDs as the FP refinement.
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate enterprise rollout of Replicon / Harvest / Toggl / Clockify / Hubstaff / TimeDoctor — allowlist their ApplicationId values
  • Microsoft Project / Dynamics 365 Time-tracking modules that share the keyword
  • Internal LOB timesheet apps registered by the HR team
  • Pen-test / red-team OAuth phishing simulations from an authorised vendor
  • Existing tenant-wide admin consent that re-triggers on user-level top-up grants
Suppression filter
| where ApplicationId !in ("<replicon-app-id>", "<harvest-app-id>", "<toggl-app-id>", "<clockify-app-id>") and Consenter !endswith "@vendor-onboarding.yourorg.com"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the ApplicationId, publisher, verified-publisher status, redirect URIs, and requested permission scopes (especially Mail.ReadWrite, Mail.Send, Files.Read.All, offline_access) from Entra ID > Enterprise applications. Check whether the consenter is a human user or an AI-agent service principal — agents auto-consenting is the article's exact concern. Step 2 — Contain: revoke the OAuth grant via 'Remove user consent' or PowerShell `Remove-AzureADOAuth2PermissionGrant`; disable the service principal; invalidate refresh tokens for the consenter via `Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken`. Step 3 — Hunt: search the last 30 days of MailItemsAccessed / Send / FileSyncDownloadedFull for the affected identity, check for inbox rules created by the app, and look for other 'timesheet'-themed app registrations across the tenant.
let TimesheetPattern = @"(?i)(time\s*sheet|time-sheet|timesheet|time\s*track|timetrack|hour\s*log|hours\s*app|punch\s*clock|timeclock|workhours)";
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType has_any ("Consent to application.", "Consent to application", "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.", "Add delegated permission grant.", "Add app role assignment grant to user.")
| extend AppName = tostring(coalesce(ObjectName, tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).ObjectName), tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).Target[0].ID)))
| extend ConsentScope = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).ModifiedProperties)
| where AppName matches regex TimesheetPattern
| project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, AccountUpn=AccountId, IPAddress, CountryCode, AppName, ApplicationId, ConsentScope, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
let TimesheetPattern = @"(?i)(time\s*sheet|time-sheet|timesheet|time\s*track|timetrack|hour\s*log|hours\s*app|punch\s*clock|timeclock|workhours)";
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OperationName in ("Consent to application", "Add delegated permission grant", "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant", "Add app role assignment grant to user")
| mv-expand TargetResources
| extend AppName = tostring(TargetResources.displayName)
| extend ModifiedProps = tostring(TargetResources.modifiedProperties)
| where AppName matches regex TimesheetPattern
| extend Consenter = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| extend ConsenterIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, AppName, Consenter, ConsenterIP, Result, ResultReason, ModifiedProps
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")

Pythagora-io/gpt-pilot Compromised on GitHub - Shai-Hulud Credential Stealer Blocked by Python Linter

2026-06-09 13 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On June 8, 2026, multiple Graph ML PyPI packages in the bioinformatics ecosystem were compromised in the Hades campaign, deploying cross-platform memory scrapers, AI prompt injections to misdirect scanners, and a token-revocation wiper.

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Hades Campaign: pip install of compromised PyPI packages and versions · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Pythagora-io/gpt-pilot Compromised on GitHub - Shai-Hulud Credential Stealer Blo
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Hades Campaign: Python drops Bun runtime to /tmp/b/ from oven-sh release · [LLM] Hades Campaign: Bun binary in /tmp/b/ executes _index.js payload · [LLM] Hades Campaign: .bun_ran flag file created in temp directory · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Hades Campaign: process reads /proc/<Runner.Worker>/mem on GitHub Actions runner · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Hades Campaign: Python drops Bun runtime to /tmp/b/ from oven-sh release AIInstallation High
Detects the Hades Campaign's stage-1 import hook: a Python interpreter (loading a compromised PyPI package's __init__.py) writing the Bun runtime ZIP and extracted binary into /tmp/b/. This is the malware's distinctive way to obtain a JS runtime in environments lacking Node. Rationale: Anchored on the exact paths from the deobfuscated __init__.py hook: `_b = _o.path.join(_T.gettempdir(), "b", "bun")` and `_z = _o.path.join(_T.gettempdir(), "b.zip")`. The Python+/tmp/b/ pairing is article-unique — legitimate Bun installs land in ~/.bun/bin/, never /tmp/b/.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer manually testing Bun under /tmp during local debugging
  • Dockerfile builds that extract Bun to /tmp inside a build stage
  • CI cache restore steps that materialize a bun binary at a /tmp path
  • Engineer following oven-sh upstream install one-liner into /tmp
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("oven-sh install","curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl","bash"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: confirm the parent Python process and which package's __init__.py triggered the import (check InitiatingProcessCommandLine working dir; correlate with pip install events in the prior 24h). Pull SHA256 of /tmp/b/bun and check VT. 2) CONTAIN: isolate the host (especially if it is a CI runner with cloud credentials), revoke any short-lived OIDC tokens issued in the runner's session, rotate AWS/Azure/GCP keys exposed to that workflow. 3) HUNT: pivot on the AccountName/DeviceId for `.bun_ran` flag-file creation (UC3), bun child process running _index.js (UC2), and any /proc/*/mem reads against Runner.Worker (UC5). Pull the compromised package list and check pip install history against UC6.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where (FolderPath has "/tmp/b/" and FileName =~ "bun")
   or (FolderPath has "/tmp" and FileName =~ "b.zip")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","python3.9","python3.10","python3.11","python3.12","pythonw.exe","unzip")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where (TargetFilePath has "/tmp/b/" and TargetFileName =~ "bun")
   or (TargetFilePath has "/tmp" and TargetFileName =~ "b.zip")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","unzip")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
title: Hades Campaign Bun Runtime Dropped to /tmp/b by Python
id: 8c5e2a14-7b3d-4f29-9c1e-2a3b4c5d6e7f
description: Detects the Hades Campaign stage-1 hook writing the Bun runtime ZIP and binary into /tmp/b/ from a Python interpreter that loaded a compromised PyPI package.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/pythagora-io-gpt-pilot-compromised-on-github-shai-hulud-credential-stealer-blocked-by-python-linter
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/10
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1059.006
  - attack.t1105
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_bun:
    TargetFilename: '/tmp/b/bun'
  selection_zip:
    TargetFilename: '/tmp/b.zip'
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
      - '/python3.9'
      - '/python3.10'
      - '/python3.11'
      - '/python3.12'
      - '/unzip'
  condition: (selection_bun or selection_zip) and selection_proc
level: high
source:linux.auditd (@auditd.type:PATH OR @auditd.type:CREATE) (@file.path:/tmp/b/bun OR @file.path:/tmp/b.zip OR @file.name:bun OR @file.name:b.zip) @process.name:(python OR python3 OR python3.9 OR python3.10 OR python3.11 OR python3.12 OR unzip)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten (TargetFileName=/^\/tmp\/b\/bun$/i OR TargetFileName=/^\/tmp\/b\.zip$/i)
| ContextImageFileName=/\/(python(3(\.\d+)?)?|unzip)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName, ContextProcessId], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action=created AND ((Filesystem.file_path="/tmp/b/bun" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/tmp/b/bun") OR (Filesystem.file_name="b.zip" AND Filesystem.file_path="/tmp/b.zip")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_path
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where process_name IN ("python","python3","python3.9","python3.10","python3.11","python3.12","unzip","bash","sh")

Hades Campaign: Bun binary in /tmp/b/ executes _index.js payload AIInstallation High
Detects the Hades Campaign stage-2: the dropped Bun runtime at /tmp/b/bun invoked with `run _index.js` to launch the modular AES-256-GCM-decrypted payload. Distinguishes from legitimate Bun by both the unusual install path and the _index.js argument. Rationale: Article verbatim: `_s.run([_b, "run", _j], env=dict(_o.environ), check=False)` where `_b = /tmp/b/bun` and `_j` is the located `_index.js`. The combo of /tmp/b/bun executable path + `_index.js` argument is article-unique; legitimate Bun never runs out of /tmp/b/.
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1027 T1140
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running Bun from a custom /tmp install during dev
  • Ephemeral container builds that stage Bun in /tmp/b/ for build steps
  • Internal CI tooling that intentionally drops Bun to /tmp/b/bun
  • Bun upstream test suites checking out under /tmp
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull SHA256 of /tmp/b/bun and compare to oven-sh-published v1.3.14 hashes — Hades campaign uses an unmodified legit Bun binary, so the file is benign in isolation; the signal is the path + _index.js arg. Inspect /tmp/_index.js content and the parent Python process's working directory to identify which PyPI package triggered it. 2) CONTAIN: kill the bun PID, isolate host, revoke any GitHub Actions OIDC tokens, rotate secrets exported to the workflow's environment variables. 3) HUNT: enumerate DNS queries from this bun PID (C2 lookup), file writes (modular blob staging), and cross-host pivot on SHA256 of /tmp/_index.js.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FolderPath has "/tmp/b" and FileName =~ "bun")
   or ProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/b/bun"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "_index.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (TargetProcessName has "/tmp/b/" and TargetProcessName endswith "/bun")
   or TargetProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/b/bun"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "_index.js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, SHA256

Hades Campaign: .bun_ran flag file created in temp directory AIInstallation High
Detects creation of the article's signature one-shot guard file `.bun_ran` in the system temp dir, written after the Bun payload runs once per boot to prevent re-execution. Extremely high-fidelity — the filename is unique to this campaign. Rationale: Article verbatim: `_G = _O.path.join(_T.gettempdir(), ".bun_ran")` and the closing line `open(_G, "w").close()`. The filename `.bun_ran` is a campaign-unique artifact — Google/grep returns no legitimate software using this exact name as a guard file.
ATT&CKT1480 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Detonation/sandbox runs of this same sample by an internal IR team
  • Threat researcher running deobfuscated POC on an instrumented box
  • Red team replaying Hades artifacts during a tabletop exercise
  • Backup/restore of a previously compromised host's /tmp
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull the ContextImageFileName/InitiatingProcess and confirm whether the writer was python (matches campaign) or bun (less common but possible). Snapshot /tmp/_index.js, /tmp/b/bun, and the Python __init__.py that triggered the hook. 2) CONTAIN: isolate host immediately — guard-file existence proves the JS payload already executed, so credential-scraping modules have run. Force rotate ALL secrets reachable from this host (cloud keys, GitHub PATs, npm tokens, deploy keys). 3) HUNT: query the affected PyPI package install history (UC6), search for the SHA256 of /tmp/_index.js across the fleet, and look for outbound to github.com from non-developer hosts (potential exfil channel — same TA pattern from prior Miasma campaigns).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ ".bun_ran"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ ".bun_ran"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          TargetFileName, TargetFilePath,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

Hades Campaign: process reads /proc/<Runner.Worker>/mem on GitHub Actions runner AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the Hades campaign's Linux credential scrape — a non-system process opening /proc/<pid>/mem or /proc/<pid>/maps where the target PID belongs to the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker process. Article confirms this is how the malware extracts plaintext secrets from in-memory environment variables. Rationale: Article describes the Linux scraper: `walks the memory mappings in /proc/{pid}/maps and directly reads /proc/{pid}/mem to scrape plaintext variables` targeting the Runner.Worker process. Correlating the file access against a live Runner.Worker PID on the same host eliminates legit observability tools that scan /proc/self/.
ATT&CKT1003.007 T1552.001 T1212
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Datadog / New Relic / Wavefront agent collecting per-process metrics from /proc
  • On-runner debugging by an SRE using gdb/strace against Runner.Worker
  • Memory-forensics tooling (volatility, lime) deliberately invoked
  • crash/coredumpctl reading /proc state after a runner crash
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("datadog-agent","newrelic-infra","telegraf","node_exporter","prometheus","falcon-sensor","mdatp")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: identify the InitiatingProcessFileName — if it's `python`, `bun`, or any process running out of /tmp/b/ this is high-confidence Hades. Capture full process tree, working dir, and parent. 2) CONTAIN: terminate the scraper PID, take the runner offline, treat ALL secrets that have ever transited this runner's env vars as compromised — rotate GitHub OIDC, npm/PyPI publish tokens, cloud keys, registry creds. 3) HUNT: pivot on the scraper SHA256 across the fleet, check for outbound GitHub API calls from this host (Miasma uses GitHub for exfil per prior advisories), and look for the same SHA256 on dev workstations that pulled the affected PyPI packages.
let RunnerWorkers = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName =~ "Runner.Worker"
    | project DeviceId, RunnerPid = tostring(ProcessId), RunnerStart = Timestamp;
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath startswith "/proc/"
| where FileName in~ ("mem","maps")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ps","top","htop","systemd","kthreadd","strace","gdb","crash")
| extend AccessedPid = extract(@"/proc/(\d+)/", 1, FolderPath)
| join kind=inner RunnerWorkers on DeviceId, $left.AccessedPid == $right.RunnerPid
| where Timestamp >= RunnerStart
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          AccessedPid, FolderPath, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
let RunnerWorkers = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where TargetProcessName has "Runner.Worker"
    | project DvcHostname, RunnerPid = tostring(TargetProcessId), RunnerStart = TimeGenerated;
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath startswith "/proc/"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("mem","maps")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("ps","top","htop","systemd","strace","gdb")
| extend AccessedPid = extract(@"/proc/(\d+)/", 1, TargetFilePath)
| join kind=inner RunnerWorkers on DvcHostname, $left.AccessedPid == $right.RunnerPid
| where TimeGenerated >= RunnerStart
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          AccessedPid, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:SYSCALL (@auditd.syscall:openat OR @auditd.syscall:open) (@file.path:/proc/*/mem OR @file.path:/proc/*/maps) -@process.name:(ps OR top OR htop OR systemd OR strace OR gdb OR crash)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo (TargetFileName=/^\/proc\/\d+\/mem$/i OR TargetFileName=/^\/proc\/\d+\/maps$/i)
| ContextImageFileName!=/\/(ps|top|htop|systemd|strace|gdb|crash)$/i
| AccessedPid := regex("/proc/(?<pid>\\d+)/", field=TargetFileName, strict=false)
| join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/Runner\.Worker$/i | RunnerPid := TargetProcessId | groupBy([aid, RunnerPid], function=min(_time))}, field=[aid], include=[RunnerPid])
| AccessedPid=RunnerPid
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName, AccessedPid], function=count())

Hades Campaign: pip install of compromised PyPI packages and versions AIDelivery High
Detects installation of one of the seven named Hades-Campaign PyPI packages at the exact affected versions (ensmallen 0.8.101, embiggen 0.11.97, gpsea 0.9.14, mflux-streamlit 0.0.3/0.0.4, nhmpy 2.4.7, ppkt2synergy 0.1.1, pyphetools 0.9.120). Alerts before payload execution if installs are scanned at command time. Rationale: Affected-version table from the article is the ground truth: each `package==version` string is a unique IOC. Pinning to `==<exact-version>` (and `-<version>` for wheel/sdist filename matches) keeps the detection alerting-tier even after the maintainers publish a patched version of the same package.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IR/threat-research team intentionally installing the malicious version in a sandbox for analysis
  • Air-gapped reproduction environment for advisory validation
  • Mirror sync of historical PyPI metadata into an internal index (manifest-only, no install)
  • Dependency-scanning tools that print the package@version string in their own logs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--dry-run" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--no-deps --download" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("sandbox.sh","hades-repro.sh")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: confirm the install actually completed (look for the matching site-packages directory write event) vs. a metadata-only resolve. Pull the user account, working dir, and pyproject.toml/requirements.txt that pinned the version. 2) CONTAIN: if install succeeded, isolate the host; treat the user's developer credentials and any creds in env vars / .aws / .npmrc / git config as compromised. If a CI runner installed it, treat the workflow's OIDC token + all repo secrets as burned. 3) HUNT: cross-reference with UC1 (Bun drop), UC3 (.bun_ran), UC5 (Runner.Worker memory scrape) on the same host; check internal PyPI mirrors / artifact repositories for cached copies of the affected versions; sweep `requirements*.txt`, `pyproject.toml`, `Pipfile.lock`, `uv.lock`, `poetry.lock` across repos for pinned references.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has_any ("pip","pip3","pip.exe","python","python3","uv","poetry")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("pip","pip3","uv","poetry")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (
    "ensmallen==0.8.101","ensmallen-0.8.101",
    "embiggen==0.11.97","embiggen-0.11.97",
    "gpsea==0.9.14","gpsea-0.9.14",
    "mflux-streamlit==0.0.3","mflux-streamlit==0.0.4",
    "mflux_streamlit-0.0.3","mflux_streamlit-0.0.4",
    "nhmpy==2.4.7","nhmpy-2.4.7",
    "ppkt2synergy==0.1.1","ppkt2synergy-0.1.1",
    "pyphetools==0.9.120","pyphetools-0.9.120"
  )
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("pip","pip3","python","python3","uv","poetry")
   or TargetProcessName has_any ("pip","pip3","uv","poetry")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any (
    "ensmallen==0.8.101","ensmallen-0.8.101",
    "embiggen==0.11.97","embiggen-0.11.97",
    "gpsea==0.9.14","gpsea-0.9.14",

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

| sort - count

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",

Miasma Worm Hits Microsoft Again: Azure Functions Action and 72 Other Repositories Disabled After Supply Chain Attack Targeting AI Coding Agents

StepSecurity
2026-06-09 12 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On June 5, 2026, the Miasma worm campaign reached Microsoft's Azure GitHub organizations. GitHub disabled 73 repositories across four Microsoft GitHub organizations after a malicious commit was pushed to the Azure/durabletask repository using a previously compromised contributor account. The attack planted configuration files that execute a credential-harvesting payload when a developer opens the repository in Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, or VS Code.
